analysis.one_liner: Separates federally insured banks from investment banking, insurance, and derivatives trading.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it sat in the Senate Banking Committee from July 2013 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would restore the Glass-Steagall wall torn down in 1999, forcing banks that hold federally insured deposits to stop underwriting securities, trading for their own profit, running hedge funds, and dealing swaps. Institutions would have five years to split those businesses apart. It would also bar an executive of a securities, insurance, or swaps firm from simultaneously running an insured bank.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. Insured deposits could no longer underwrite or absorb losses from risky trading, and the implicit expectation that the government rescues Wall Street giants would shrink. The bill's stated purposes are protecting taxpayers and removing government guarantees for high-risk activities outside core banking [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions from affiliating with, being commonly owned with, or acting as insurance companies, securities entities, or swaps entities, with existing combinations terminated within five years [S2].

Bars national banks from underwriting securities or trading for their own account, limits them to core banking (deposits, credit, payments), and bans investment in structured or synthetic products [S2].
Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that let financial holding companies combine banking with securities and insurance activities [S2][S3].

Bars bank holding companies from proprietary trading, owning hedge funds or private equity funds, market-making, and prime brokerage, while letting them keep using swaps as an end user to hedge interest-rate and currency risk [S2].

Repeals special bankruptcy protections that let counterparties of financial firms immediately liquidate, terminate, or accelerate swaps, repos, and securities contracts, which in a failure lets those firms grab assets ahead of others [S2][S3].

Includes anti-evasion penalties: regulators must order termination of disguised violations, impose a penalty equal to 10 percent of the firm's three-year average net profits, and publish annual reports naming evaders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest universal banks and their shareholders. Institutions like Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase, built by merging commercial banking with securities and insurance after the 1999 repeal, would have to shed or separate those businesses within five years [S3]. Consumers could lose some one-stop financial shopping, and bank stocks could absorb the cost of the split.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large universal banks and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The five-year unwind of existing affiliations would be a massive restructuring; diversified financial firms would shed businesses, and some economists argue smaller combined institutions mean less one-stop convenience for customers and potentially less capacity to lend across business cycles (a common objection the bill text does not address) [S3].

Dodd-Frank had already imposed the Volcker rule restricting proprietary trading and fund ownership by banks; critics argued a full Glass-Steagall separation was redundant and would not by itself have prevented the 2008 failures (which involved institutions the original law did not cover, like Lehman Brothers and AIG). This is general knowledge about the policy debate, not from the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — cutting the web of explicit and implicit federal guarantees behind Wall Street's riskiest activities — is large but indirect, and its design is more workable than critics allow: it gives five years plus extensions for unwinding, exempts customer-facing trust activities, permits end-user hedging, and adds anti-evasion penalties [S3]. The honest cost is transition disruption at the largest banks and the loss of bundled services, and the bill alone would not cover every channel of financial risk. But its main burden falls on the shareholders and managements of the biggest banks, not on depositors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and read twice, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 11, 2013, joined by original cosponsors John McCain, Maria Cantwell, and Angus King [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
The complete action history shows no further action after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 113th Congress [S5].
The bill drew nine cosponsors in addition to the sponsor: six Democrats, one Republican, and two independents [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest universal banks. Because the bill died without a hearing or vote, they kept the combined commercial, investment, and insurance structure Gramm-Leach-Bliley allowed, along with insured deposits backing trading operations and the market's assumption of government support for too-big-to-fail firms [S3].

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. John McCain, Maria Cantwell, and Angus King
for.role: Original cosponsors (one Republican, one Democrat, one independent)
for.what_they_did: Joined as the three other original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Six Senate Democrats and two independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total sponsorship to nine cosponsors plus the sponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Major financial institutions and their trade groups
against.role: The largest universal banks whose structure the bill would unwind
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstating the Glass-Steagall separation, which would force them to break apart businesses assembled after the 1999 repeal; this opposition was widely reported but does not appear in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — six Democrats, one Republican (Sen. McCain), and two independents — but the committee never acted, so no vote exists to measure the parties' split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill forces them to end affiliations between insured deposits and securities, insurance, and swaps businesses within five years, and repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that created them. Their cost is shareholders' and managements'; the public's gain is removing insured deposits and implicit bailouts from trading risk.

industries.industry: Securities and investment banking arms of banks
industries.note: Underwriting, market-making, prime brokerage, and proprietary trading would be barred for bank holding companies and banks. Independent securities firms outside the banking system keep operating; the loss is to the merged giants.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds backed by banks
industries.note: Banks could no longer own, sponsor, or invest in them, cutting off a source of bank-subsidized capital. The funds themselves, if independent, are unaffected.

industries.industry: Community banks and independent financial firms
industries.note: A level playing field: they already operate without combined trading-and-deposit empires, and the bill's ban on structured products and underwriting removes subsidized competition from giants perceived as too big to fail.
